title: Chemical equilibrium
summary: Dynamic equilibrium, K and Q, Le Chatelier's principle and the solubility product.
cards.0.p: In a closed container many reactions run in both directions (⇌). When the forward and reverse rates become equal, equilibrium is reached. At this point the concentrations no longer change, but they don't have to be equal.
cards.0.svg#12: Rates equal; concentrations constant but not equal
cards.0.key: Equilibrium is reached only in a closed system. The water–vapor equilibrium and a saturated solution are physical equilibria.
cards.1.p: For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD we write Kc = [C]c[D]d / [A]a[B]b. Products go in the numerator and reactants in the denominator. Solids and pure liquids are left out.
cards.1.svg#12: Solids (s) and pure liquids (l) are not written in the expression.
cards.1.key: As long as the temperature doesn't change, Kc stays constant. Gases and (aq) species go into the expression, but substances in (s) and (l) states don't.
cards.1.once.soru: For CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g), which substance appears in the Kc expression?
cards.1.once.secenekler.0.neden: The concentration of a solid is constant and isn't written in the expression. So Kc = [CO₂].
cards.1.once.secenekler.1.neden: CaCO₃ and CaO are solids, so they don't go into the K expression.
cards.1.once.secenekler.2.neden: Solids are left out, and gases are written.
cards.2.h: The relationship between Kp and Kc
cards.2.p: For gas reactions, K can also be written with partial pressures, and this is called Kp. Kp = Kc·(RT)Δn. Here Δn is the moles of gaseous products minus the moles of gaseous reactants.
cards.2.svg#6: Δn = moles of gaseous products − moles of gaseous reactants
cards.2.svg#28: Solids and liquids are not counted in Δn.
cards.2.key: T is in kelvins, and only gases are counted in Δn. Partial pressure is the pressure a gas would exert on its own in the mixture.
cards.2.once.soru: In H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI, the moles of gas are equal on both sides. How are Kp and Kc related?
cards.3.h: What does the size of K tell us?
cards.3.p: If K is very large, products dominate at equilibrium and the reaction almost goes to completion. If K is very small, reactants remain the majority. K says nothing about the rate of the reaction.
cards.3.svg#12: K gives no information about the reaction rate.
cards.3.key: Roughly, if K > 10³, products dominate. A large K means a lot of product, not a fast reaction.
cards.3.once.soru: A reaction has K = 10¹⁰. What can be said about this reaction?
cards.3.once.secenekler.0.neden: A large K shows that the numerator, the products, dominate.
cards.3.once.secenekler.1.neden: K says nothing about rate. Reaching equilibrium could take years.
cards.3.once.secenekler.2.neden: That happens when K is very small.
cards.4.p: If the equation is reversed, the new constant is 1/K. If the coefficients are multiplied by n, it becomes Kn. If two equations are added, the constants are multiplied to give K1·K2.
cards.4.svg#13: (1) and (2) are two equations with constants K₁ and K₂.
cards.4.key: If the coefficients are halved, it becomes √K. When equations are added, the Ks are multiplied, not added.
cards.4.once.soru: For A ⇌ B, K = 4. What is K for B ⇌ A?
cards.4.once.secenekler.0.neden: In the reverse reaction the numerator and denominator swap. So K' = 1/K.
cards.4.once.secenekler.1.neden: When the equation is reversed, the expression is inverted too.
cards.4.once.secenekler.2.neden: K is a ratio of concentrations and can't be negative.
cards.5.p: Writing the current concentrations into the K expression gives Q. If Q < K, the reaction runs forward, and if Q > K, it runs in reverse. If Q = K, the system is at equilibrium.
cards.5.svg#0: Q: current concentrations in the K expression
cards.5.etk.soru: H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI, K<sub>c</sub> = 64 at this temperature. Change the current concentrations: Q = [HI]²/([H₂][I₂]) tells the direction of the reaction.
cards.5.etk.yorum.0.1: Q < K: the reaction runs forward.
cards.5.etk.yorum.1.1: Q = K: the system is at equilibrium.
cards.5.etk.yorum.2.1: Q > K: the reaction runs in reverse.
cards.5.key: A reaction always moves in the direction that brings Q closer to K.
cards.6.p: For an equilibrium calculation, set up a table with rows for initial, change and equilibrium. The changes are proportional to the coefficients. For example, for H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI the changes are −x, −x and +2x. Concentrations go into K.
cards.6.key: If the container isn't 1 L, divide moles by volume. For example, if a 2 L container starts with 2 mol each of H₂ and I₂ and 2.4 mol of HI forms at equilibrium, then x = 1.2. In that case Kc = 1.2² / 0.4² = 9.
cards.7.p: According to Le Chatelier's principle, if a system at equilibrium is disturbed, the equilibrium shifts in the direction that reduces the disturbance. If a substance is added, it shifts toward the side that uses it up. If a substance is removed, it shifts toward the side that produces it.
cards.7.svg#9: The temperature is the same, so K doesn't change.
cards.7.key: If the temperature is constant, K doesn't change. Adding a solid or a pure liquid doesn't shift the equilibrium.
cards.7.once.soru: You add some more of a reactant to a container at equilibrium. Which way does the equilibrium shift?
cards.7.once.secenekler.0.neden: The equilibrium shifts toward the side that uses up the added substance, which is forward.
cards.7.once.secenekler.1.neden: The reverse direction produces reactants. That would increase the excess substance even more.
cards.7.once.secenekler.2.neden: Adding a gaseous or dissolved reactant does shift the equilibrium.
cards.8.p: At constant temperature, when the volume shrinks the pressure rises, and the equilibrium shifts toward the side with fewer moles of gas. If the moles are equal, there is no shift. Adding an inert gas at constant volume doesn't shift the equilibrium either.
cards.8.etk.soru: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), ΔH = −92 kJ. For each change, which way does the equilibrium shift?
cards.8.etk.ogeler.2.2: The pressure rises. The equilibrium shifts toward the side with fewer moles of gas (2 mol NH₃).
cards.8.etk.ogeler.3.2: The reaction is exothermic. When the temperature rises, the equilibrium shifts toward the heat-absorbing direction, which is reverse.
cards.8.etk.ogeler.5.2: The pressure falls. The equilibrium shifts toward the side with more moles of gas (4 mol).
cards.8.etk.ogeler.6.2: A catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse reactions by the same factor.
cards.8.etk.ogeler.7.2: The partial pressures don't change, so the equilibrium doesn't shift.
cards.8.key: If an inert gas is added at constant pressure, the volume grows. Then the equilibrium shifts toward the side with more moles.
cards.9.p: Only temperature changes K. Heating shifts the equilibrium in the endothermic direction. So for an exothermic reaction K decreases, and for an endothermic one it increases. A catalyst doesn't shift the equilibrium.
cards.9.key: For an exothermic reaction, heating speeds it up but makes K smaller.
cards.10.p: Ammonia is made from N₂ and H₂. The reaction is exothermic and the moles of gas decrease. So high pressure raises the yield. A temperature of about 450 °C and an iron catalyst are a compromise between rate and yield.
cards.10.svg#9: unreacted N₂ and H₂ are recycled
cards.10.svg#10: High P: shifts to fewer-moles side (NH₃), yield rises
cards.10.svg#11: Low T raises yield but is slow: 450 °C is a compromise
cards.10.key: A low temperature raises the yield, but the reaction becomes very slow. Cooling NH₃ and removing it pushes the equilibrium toward the products.
cards.11.p: A slightly soluble salt is in equilibrium with its ions in a saturated solution. For AgCl we write Ksp = [Ag+][Cl−]. If the solubility is s, Ksp = s² for AB type salts and 4s³ for AB₂ type.
cards.11.key: Ksp is short for solubility product. You can compare Ksp and solubility directly only for salts of the same type.
cards.11.once.soru: In the equilibrium AgCl(s) ⇌ Ag⁺ + Cl⁻, why isn't AgCl written in the Ksp expression?
cards.11.once.secenekler.0.neden: The concentration of a solid is constant and isn't written in the K expression.
cards.11.once.secenekler.1.neden: It's left out because it is a solid, not because it dissolves slightly.
cards.11.once.secenekler.2.neden: Dissolved ions are written. What is left out is the solid form of the substance.
cards.12.p: If the ion product in a mixture is Q > Ksp, a precipitate forms. If one of the salt's ions is already in the solution (a common ion), the salt dissolves less.
cards.12.svg#9: Common ion effect: solubility of AgCl (25 °C)
cards.12.svg#14: Extra Cl⁻ pushes the equilibrium left, so AgCl dissolves less.
cards.12.key: If Q = Ksp, the solution is saturated. When solutions are mixed, the volume grows. So calculate Q with the diluted concentrations.
cards.12.once.soru: Can you dissolve more AgCl in pure water or in NaCl solution?
cards.12.once.secenekler.0.neden: The Cl⁻ in NaCl pushes the equilibrium left. So AgCl dissolves less in that solution.
cards.12.once.secenekler.1.neden: The common Cl⁻ ion lowers solubility, it doesn't raise it.
cards.13.p:
• At equilibrium the forward and reverse rates are equal and concentrations are constant.
• Solids and pure liquids are not written in the K expression.
• If Q < K the reaction runs forward, and if Q > K it runs in reverse.
• Equilibrium shifts in the direction that reduces the disturbance, and only temperature changes K.
• If Q > Ksp, a precipitate forms. A common ion lowers solubility.
cards.13.svg#11: Solids and pure liquids are not written in the K expression.
quiz.0.q: At constant temperature, 1 mol of N₂O₄ is placed in a closed 2 L container: N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g). At equilibrium the container holds 0.4 mol of NO₂. What is K<sub>c</sub>?
quiz.0.e: When 0.4 mol of NO₂ forms, 0.2 mol of N₂O₄ is used up and 0.8 mol of N₂O₄ remains. [N₂O₄] = 0.4 M and [NO₂] = 0.2 M, so K<sub>c</sub> = 0.2² / 0.4 = 0.1.
quiz.1.q: The reaction N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) is exothermic. Sort each change by where it shifts the equilibrium.
quiz.1.e: Added N₂ is used up, and removed NH₃ is produced again. When the volume shrinks, the equilibrium shifts toward the side with fewer moles (2 mol gas). Heating shifts an exothermic equilibrium toward the reactants. A catalyst and He added at constant volume don't shift the equilibrium.
quiz.2.q: In a saturated solution of a slightly soluble AB<sub>2</sub> salt, the molar solubility is s = 1×10<sup>−3</sup> M. What is K<sub>sp</sub>?
quiz.2.y.0: You used s² as for the AB type. AB<sub>2</sub> has two anions, so the result is 4s³.
quiz.2.y.1: You forgot to square 2s. The right answer is s·(2s)² = 4s³.
quiz.2.y.3: You used just s³. [B<sup>−</sup>] = 2s, so its square is 4s², and the result is 4s³.
quiz.3.q: For A(g) + B(g) ⇌ 2C(g), K<sub>c</sub> = 4 at a certain temperature. At one moment a 1 L container holds 1 mol of A, 1 mol of B and 4 mol of C. Which is true?
quiz.3.o.3: It runs in reverse, C decreases
quiz.3.e: Q = 4² / (1·1) = 16. Since Q > K, the reaction runs in reverse. C is used up until Q drops to 4.
quiz.3.y.0: Q = [C]²/([A][B]) = 4²/(1·1) = 16. Since Q ≠ K, the system is not at equilibrium.
quiz.3.y.1: Q = 16, which is larger than K = 4. There is too much product, so the reaction runs in reverse.
quiz.3.y.2: When calculating Q, [C] must be squared. So the result is 4² = 16, not 4.
A:ozet: Watch equilibrium form and calculate Kc. Compare Q with K, then push the equilibrium with pressure, temperature and a catalyst.
A:adimlar.0.metin: We put only N₂O₄ into a closed container, and the reaction N₂O₄ ⇌ 2NO₂ begins. Watch the forward and reverse rates.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.soru: What happens when the rates become equal?
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: From outside it looks stopped, but the molecules keep converting. Equilibrium isn't static, it is dynamic.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: The conversion continues, but the two directions balance each other. This is called dynamic equilibrium. You would reach equilibrium even if you started with only NO₂.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The reverse reaction makes N₂O₄ again from NO₂. In a closed container the reactants don't run out.
A:adimlar.1.metin: We put 1 mol each of H₂ and I₂ into a 1 L container. At equilibrium 1.6 mol of HI was measured. Adjust the table to match.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.ipucu: While 2x mol of HI forms, x mol of H₂ and x mol of I₂ are used up.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.tamam: 2x = 1.6, so x = 0.8. At equilibrium there is 0.2 M H₂, 0.2 M I₂ and 1.6 M HI. Kc = 1.6² / (0.2 · 0.2) = 64.
A:adimlar.2.metin: Writing the current concentrations into the K expression gives Q. For H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI, K = 64, and the container has [H₂] = [I₂] = 0.1 M. Find the HI concentration that makes Q equal to K.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.tamam: Q = 0.8² / (0.1 · 0.1) = 64, which equals K. So the system is at equilibrium. If Q < K the reaction runs forward, and if Q > K it runs in reverse.
A:adimlar.3.metin: The reaction N₂O₄ ⇌ 2NO₂ is at equilibrium. We push the piston to halve the volume.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.soru: Which way does the equilibrium shift?
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: There are 2 mol of gas on the right. If the equilibrium shifted there, the moles of gas and the pressure would rise. The system does the opposite.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: The moles of gas differ on the two sides, so a volume change shifts the equilibrium.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: To lower the pressure, the system lowers the moles of gas, and 2 mol of NO₂ turn into 1 mol of N₂O₄. But it doesn't erase the disturbance completely. The NO₂ concentration still stays higher than at the start.
A:adimlar.4.metin: We put 1 M N₂O₄ into a closed container, and the reaction N₂O₄ + heat ⇌ 2NO₂ began. NO₂ is brown. Watch the molecules and the concentration graph. Then add N₂O₄ to the container or heat it.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.bulgular.0.yazi: Watch equilibrium form. Why don't the concentrations change anymore?
A:adimlar.4.gorev.bulgular.0.tamam: The forward and reverse rates became equal. The reaction didn't stop, it runs both ways at the same rate. So the concentrations stayed constant and dynamic equilibrium was reached.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.bulgular.1.yazi: At equilibrium, add N₂O₄ and wait for the new equilibrium.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.bulgular.1.tamam: Some of the added N₂O₄ turned into NO₂. The equilibrium shifted forward, the direction that uses up the added substance (Le Chatelier). Q became equal to K again, and K didn't change.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.bulgular.2.yazi: Heat the container above 360 K and wait for the new equilibrium.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.bulgular.2.tamam: The forward direction absorbs heat. So heating shifted the equilibrium forward, the container turned brown and Kc grew. Only temperature changes K.
A:adimlar.5.metin: Add a catalyst to the same reaction and compare the NO₂ curves.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.soru: How does a catalyst affect equilibrium?
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: A catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally. The equilibrium concentrations and K don't change, only the time to reach equilibrium gets shorter.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Both curves rise to the same height. A catalyst doesn't increase product or shift the equilibrium.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: K changes only with temperature. A catalyst speeds up both directions equally, so it doesn't change the ratio.
A:adimlar.6.metin: Look at the reaction N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ + heat. Change the pressure and temperature, then look at the NH₃ yield and the rate.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.soru: Which raises the NH₃ yield without lowering the rate?
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: The rate rises, but the forward direction is exothermic, so the equilibrium shifts left and the yield drops.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: In the reaction 4 mol of gas turn into 2 mol. So pressure shifts the equilibrium toward NH₃, the side with fewer moles. Compressed gases also collide more, so the rate doesn't drop.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The yield rises, but the reaction becomes very slow. That's why a moderate temperature and a catalyst are chosen.
A:kapanis.0: In a closed container, when the forward and reverse rates become equal, dynamic equilibrium is reached. Concentrations stay constant, but conversion continues.
A:kapanis.1: Kc is the ratio of product concentrations to reactant concentrations, with the coefficients as exponents. Solids and pure liquids are not written in it.
A:kapanis.2: If Q < K the reaction runs forward, and if Q > K it runs in reverse. If Q = K, the system is at equilibrium.
A:kapanis.3: By Le Chatelier's principle, a system reduces the disturbance. When pressure rises, the equilibrium shifts toward fewer moles of gas, and when heated, toward the endothermic direction.
A:kapanis.4: Only temperature changes K. A catalyst speeds up reaching equilibrium, but it doesn't shift it.
